summary: Deep dive on Mariner's VPC/on-prem private deployment needs — focus on airlock (ingress/egress), egress proxy patterns, KMS integration, and audit/logging requirements. Redwood AE + SE walked through tradeoffs for tight egress allowlists, NAT gateway vs egress proxy, and options for HSM-backed KMS in customer network.
topics: Network isolation: subnets, host zoning, and microsegmentation
Ingress controls: limited management plane access and bastion patterns
Egress controls: proxy vs NAT, allowlist maintenance, deep packet inspection concerns
Key management: bring-your-own-KMS, HSM integration, envelope encryption
Auditability: immutable audit logs, syscall-level telemetry vs app logs
Compliance mapping: SOC 2 evidence areas, ISO/IEC 27001 considerations
Operational runbooks: incident response, rotation, and onboarding checklist
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Maya H., Owen P. (Redwood) — Elias J., Priya K., Daniel W. (Mariner)

Summary note: audio had occasional dropouts around 00:47:00, transcription may mislabel speakers in a few places.

[00:00:08] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, i know you had a packed week so we'll try to be efficient; i'm maya, i'm the account lead, and with me is owen, our solutions eng
[00:00:18] Elias: hey maya, thanks, this is elias — happy to get into the weeds. priya and daniel are on as well
[00:00:23] Priya: hi all
[00:00:26] Daniel: hey folks
[00:00:30] Owen: quick agenda — network isolation and airlock patterns, egress strategy, kms and encryption handshake, audit logs and evidence, then open q and next steps
[00:01:02] Priya: to set context, we've got a hybrid estate — primary workloads in GCP us-central, some on prem for regulated data. we're evaluating Redwood Private in a VPC-first deploy. main constraints are: egress must be filtered to a small allowlist, key custody via our HSM, and audit logs retained for 3 years for SOC2/ISO audits
[00:01:28] Maya: got it. when you say allowlist can you ballpark how tight? dozens of endpoints or a few static ip ranges?
[00:01:36] Priya: more like a few CIDR blocks — third party dependencies are limited, it's mostly our telemetry and a small set of model repo endpoints
[00:01:44] Elias: and we can't have uncontrolled DNS resolution to arbitrary domains, that's a hard no from security
[00:01:50] Owen: yeah that's common. two patterns we recommend: 1) a strict egress proxy / outbound gateway in your VPC that does TLS-inspection and allowlists, or 2) NAT plus strict security group + route tables with stateful firewalling. each has tradeoffs
[00:02:08] [00:02:09] Owen: the proxy gives you better control and observability, but introduces a single egress hop and requires scaling; NAT is simpler but less inspectable
[00:02:35] Daniel: could you expand on TLS inspection — we have privacy concerns for PII in payloads, not sure we can terminate TLS in our proxy
[00:02:46] Owen: right, you can use a metadata-only proxy that just enforces SNI and IP allowlists without terminating TLS; for deeper policy you'd need a TLS-termination box which then needs its own certs and audit controls. another option is an allowlist combined with mTLS between redwood nodes and your egress proxy
[00:03:10] Priya: mTLS sounds promising. how does key rotation look? we have HSM-based KMS on prem (Thales) and they require annual rotation windows
[00:03:19] Maya: we support BYOK — our control plane can be configured to call out to your KMS via customer-managed endpoints. we also support envelope encryption so the root key stays in your HSM and only ephemeral keys are used in the runtime
[00:03:32] [00:03:33] Owen: small note — sometimes the transcript says "kay-em-ess" for KMS, sorry if that shows weirdly
[00:03:40] Elias: ha, noted. on logging: we need immutable audit logs for requests and admin actions, ideally forwarded to our SIEM. do you push logs to a customer-owned S3 or to a syslog/collector?
[00:03:52] Maya: for Private we can ship structured audit events to your collector over TLS, or you can pull from a tenant-specific bucket. retention policies can be set by you; we can also provide sequences for log signing if you need tamper evidence
[00:04:12] Priya: what about operational incidents — if a node tries to egress to a non-allowed host, i want an alert and an automated quarantining of that instance
[00:04:22] Owen: that's doable — we can integrate with your orchestration to mark the instance and spin up a replacement. we emit a policy-violation webhook and create an audit event with context including payload hash and K V cache id (note — transcripts may show K V as K-space-V)
[00:04:44] Daniel: curious about the control plane — does Redwood control any internet-facing endpoints within our VPC? we need to ensure no tunnel back to redwood-managed subnets
[00:04:53] Maya: important question — for Private we run a customer-controlled control plane: the management endpoints are in your VPC (we provide images and configs), and only optional telemetry can be forwarded; there's no implicit inbound tunnel to Redwood's infra unless you opt into an outbound gateway to our support channel
[00:05:12] [00:05:13] Elias: ok, can you show a sketch of the recommended airlock?
[00:05:16] Owen: sure — imagine three zones: management (private APIs, admin), inference (model serving), and egress (proxy/bastion). Strict routing: inference nodes have no direct internet route, they talk to egress proxy on port 443 with mTLS. admin plane sits in management subnet accessible only from customer bastion with MFA and SAML SSO enforced
[00:05:39] Priya: for SSO we use Okta SAML with SCIM for user provisioning; RBAC needs to be fine-grained — can Redwood map Okta groups to roles at the token level?
[00:05:50] Maya: yes, we can map SAML attributes to RBAC roles; we also have token scoping so you can pin permissions to a particular model route or environment
[00:06:03] [00:06:04] Owen: note on network ACLs: if you need defence-in-depth, put host-based firewall rules (iptables/firewalld) on nodes plus security groups in cloud. it avoids one misconfigured SG from opening up everything
[00:06:20] Daniel: latency — adding a proxy will add ~20-80ms outbound depending on inspection. that's tolerable for non-interactive batch, but for low-latency 50ms SLAs that's a problem
[00:06:32] Owen: totally. we recommend split routing: latency-sensitive inference can use a pre-approved low-latency whitelist, while non-critical calls go through the full inspection path. or use transparent pass-through for specific model weights hosted locally
[00:06:49] Priya: about data residency — some datasets cannot leave our on-prem cluster even transiently. do you support running entire runtime on prem without any egress?
[00:06:58] Maya: yes — an airgapped private deployment is supported. in that case, the control plane is also customer-hosted and all model artifacts are stored on your NFS/block store; optional periodic signing manifests can be pulled through an approved jump host for updates
[00:07:17] [00:07:18] Elias: can we do image attestations with cosign or similar, integrate with your rollout?
[00:07:22] Owen: we currently have a workflow that accepts OCI signatures; cosign is supported as part of the onboarding spec. we can force attestation checks at deploy time
[00:07:33] Priya: SOC 2 — what artifacts will Redwood provide? we need control narratives, runbooks, and a collection of evidence to map to our auditor's checklist
[00:07:42] Maya: we provide a SOC2 artifact bundle for Private customers: control descriptions, config export, access logs, change history, and incident timelines. note though auditors sometimes ask for raw telemetry — we'll coordinate to give you necessary exports while preserving PII redaction options
[00:07:59] [00:08:00] Daniel: what's your recommended approach for KMS integration if we require HSM in our VPC and FIPS 140-2?
[00:08:08] Owen: best is to use envelope encryption: your HSM holds the root KEK; runtime nodes request ephemeral keys via a signed request to your KMS. Redwood never has the plaintext root key. For FIPS, ensure your KMS provider and algorithms are FIPS-certified and we will default to FIPS-approved ciphers on that path
[00:08:29] Priya: slightly worried about perf: if every token generation makes a KMS call for a wrapping key, that'll kill throughput
[00:08:37] Owen: agreed — we use ephemeral key caching: the runtime caches wrapped ephemeral keys per node and reuses them for many requests until expiry. only the initial unwrap hits the KMS, not per-token
[00:08:52] Elias: ok that helps. question on egress logging: we need per-request context including user id, model id, prompt hash; can that be part of the audit event forwarded to our SIEM?
[00:09:02] Maya: yes we emit structured events with those fields. we can also include deterministic prompt hashes to allow repro while avoiding storing raw PII text if that's your policy
[00:09:15] [00:09:16] Priya: what about retention — can we set S3 lifecycle to enforce 3 year retention with immutability windows for audit periods?
[00:09:25] Owen: yes S3 object lock + legal hold patterns work. we can configure the export to go to a customer bucket with object lock enabled. Redwood's control plane just writes the objects, you own retention policies
[00:09:38] Daniel: any gotchas with multi-region fallbacks? we want regional isolation guarantees but also failover in emergencies
[00:09:47] Maya: you can pin regions per deployment; for failover we suggest read-only replicas in another region and an egress policy that remains strict. automated failover needs an approved runbook because cross-region copies may violate residency controls
[00:10:05] [00:10:06] Elias: can we walk through a failure scenario — say a node attempts prohibited egress and we want to lockdown that tenant without downtime across the fleet
[00:10:15] Owen: the flow is: detection (policy violation), webhook to orchestration, mark the node as quarantined, drain traffic, spin up replacement nodes that use a policy revision that enforces stricter egress. we can also toggle model routing to an isolated fallback model to preserve service while containment happens
[00:10:36] Priya: ok. who owns the egress proxy image lifecycle? we need security patch windows and CVE management
[00:10:44] Maya: if the proxy runs in customer space, you own patching; Redwood can provide signed images and a patch cadence recommendation. for fully-managed proxy (if you choose Redwood-managed), we provide patch SLAs and CVE notifications but that implies you accept an external dependency for that component
[00:11:05] Daniel: what's the recommended approach for firewall rules between subnets — do you prefer allowlists per service port, or a default deny with a small set of service endpoints?
[00:11:14] Owen: default deny is best. allow only specific ports and mTLS endpoints. also use security group tags to limit human error when changing rules — reduce blast radius
[00:11:25] [00:11:26] Priya: curious if Redwood supports tokenized prompt redaction at ingest so PII never persists in logs even in hashed form
[00:11:34] Owen: we have an ingestion hook that can redact or tokenize fields before they hit storage; the tradeoff is it may affect evals and debug. we recommend tokenizing with a reversible mapping kept in your HSM if you need to debug under strict access control
[00:11:54] Maya: quick check on timelines — mariner, are you targeting a pilot before end of q2?
[00:12:01] Elias: yes we'd like a small pilot by mid-june, ideally 4-6 nodes and a controlled traffic profile
[00:12:07] Maya: great, we'll align the action items.
[00:12:10] [00:12:11] -- silence and discussion of internals (audio glitch) --
[00:47:12] [00:47:13] Speaker 3: (intermittent) i'm seeing a question about nginx vs envoy for the proxy
[00:47:19] Owen: envoy for dynamic routing and observability; envoy supports listener filters for SNI and mTLS better than nginx in our experience
[00:47:29] Priya: will envoy handle both SNI-only allowlists and full TLS termination?
[00:47:33] Owen: yes both. you can run envoy in a pass-through mode or full termination. we usually recommend pass-through with SNI + mTLS unless you need payload inspection
[00:48:03] Elias: small nit — our security team will want to run periodic packet-capture for incident analysis. is that compatible with your runtime hooks?
[00:48:12] Maya: yes you can mount a packet capture sidecar or mirror traffic to a collector. we can also provide higher-level traces if you prefer not to capture raw packets
[00:48:24] Daniel: last question on backup of keys — if HSM loses availability we want fallback to a secondary HSM in another AZ without exposing root keys
[00:48:33] Owen: multi-HSM replication via your KMS is the recommended approach; we only store wrapped keys so failover just points at the secondary KMS and unwrapping proceeds with the same logic
[00:48:45] Priya: thanks, that's reassuring
[00:48:49] Maya: ok let's wrap with concrete next steps: i'll share the reference architecture + SOC2 mapping by friday, owen will schedule the pilot provisioning, and priya will share firewall/allowlist details. any objections?
[00:49:05] Priya: none from me
[00:49:07] Elias: good
[00:49:09] Daniel: good to go
[00:49:12] Maya: perfect, thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff
[01:18:00] End of recording
